```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(modelr)

set.seed(1)

dir.create("plots", showWarnings = FALSE)
```


## Problem 1

Import and clean the WP homicide data.

```{r}
homicide_df =
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv", na = c("", "NA", "Unknown")) |>
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, ", ", state),
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
  ) |>
  filter(
    !(city_state %in% c("Dallas, TX", "Phoenix, AZ", "Kansas City, MO", "Tulsa, AL")),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black")
  ) |>
  mutate(victim_race = fct_relevel(victim_race, "White")) |>
  select(city_state, resolved, victim_age, victim_race, victim_sex)
```

The cleaned dataset has `r nrow(homicide_df)` homicides in `r n_distinct(pull(homicide_df, city_state))` cities. Key variables are `city_state`, `resolved` (1 = closed by arrest), `victim_age`, `victim_race` (White / Black) and `victim_sex`.

Fit the logistic regression for Baltimore.

```{r}
baltimore_fit =
  homicide_df |>
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD") |>
  glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race, data = _, family = binomial())

baltimore_or =
  baltimore_fit |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    ci_lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    ci_upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)
  ) |>
  select(term, OR, ci_lower, ci_upper, p.value)

baltimore_or |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**Sex and solving homicides in Baltimore:**

OR = `r round(pull(baltimore_or, OR), 3)`, 95% CI: (`r round(pull(baltimore_or, ci_lower), 3)`, `r round(pull(baltimore_or, ci_upper), 3)`), p < 0.001.

Therefore, keeping age and race fixed, homicides with male victims have lower odds of being solved than those with female victims.

Now fit the model for each city.

```{r}
city_or_df =
  homicide_df |>
  nest(data = -city_state) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(data, \(df) glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race, data = df, family = binomial())),
    results = map(fits, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(city_state, results) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    ci_lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    ci_upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)
  ) |>
  select(city_state, OR, ci_lower, ci_upper)

city_or_df |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Plot the ORs and CIs.

```{r, fig.asp = 1.2}
city_or_plot =
  city_or_df |>
  mutate(city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, OR)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = city_state, y = OR)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted OR for solving homicides \n (male vs female victims)",
    x = "City",
    y = "Odds ratio (95% CI)"
  )

city_or_plot

ggsave("plots/city_or_plot.png", city_or_plot, width = 8, height = 10)
```

Most cities have OR below 1, so homicides with male victims are generally less likely to be solved than those with female victims. New York has the lowest OR (0.262), while Albuquerque has the highest (1.767). Many CIs cross 1, and cities with high ORs (e.g. Albuquerque, Stockton, Fresno) have wide CIs, likely due to small samples.

## Problem 2

Load the Central Park weather data.

```{r}
data("weather_df")

weather_df =
  weather_df |>
  filter(name == "CentralPark_NY") |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin, prcp)
```

The data have `r nrow(weather_df)` daily observations from Central Park, including `date`, `prcp`, `tmax` and `tmin`.

Draw 5000 bootstrap samples, fit the model, and get r^2 and the product of the two slopes.

```{r}
boot_df =
  weather_df |>
  modelr::bootstrap(n = 5000) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(strap, \(df) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = df)),
    glance_res = map(fits, broom::glance),
    tidy_res = map(fits, broom::tidy),
    r_squared = map_dbl(glance_res, \(df) pull(df, r.squared)),
    beta_product = map_dbl(
      tidy_res,
      \(df) df |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> pull(estimate) |> prod()
    )
  ) |>
  select(.id, r_squared, beta_product)
```

Plot the distributions.

```{r}
boot_plot =
  boot_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    r_squared:beta_product,
    names_to = "quantity",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~quantity, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap distributions (5000 samples)",
    x = "Estimate",
    y = "Density"
  )

boot_plot

ggsave("plots/boot_plot.png", boot_plot, width = 8, height = 5)
```

The distribution of r^2 is unimodal and slightly left-skewed, peaking around 0.915, so tmin and prcp explain most of the variation in tmax. The distribution of the slope product is also unimodal, peaking around -0.002 with a slight right tail, because the prcp slope is very small and close to 0.

95% CIs from the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles:

```{r}
boot_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    r_squared:beta_product,
    names_to = "quantity",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |>
  group_by(quantity) |>
  summarize(
    ci_lower = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
    ci_upper = quantile(estimate, 0.975)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

The 95% CI for r^2 is (0.894, 0.928), and the 95% CI for the slope product is (-0.0051, 0.0012). Therefore, the model fits the data well, and the product of the two slopes is not clearly different from 0, since its CI includes 0.


## Problem 3

Load and clean the birthweight data.

```{r}
bwt_df =
  read_csv("data/birthweight.csv") |>
  mutate(
    babysex = factor(babysex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("male", "female")),
    frace = factor(
      frace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9),
      labels = c("White", "Black", "Asian", "Puerto Rican", "Other", "Unknown")),
    mrace = factor(
      mrace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8),
      labels = c("White", "Black", "Asian", "Puerto Rican", "Other")),
    malform = factor(malform, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("absent", "present"))
  )
```

Check missing data.

```{r}
bwt_df |>
  summarize(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  filter(n_missing > 0)
```

The data have `r nrow(bwt_df)` children and `r ncol(bwt_df)` variables, with no missing values. `babysex`, `frace`, `mrace` and `malform` are converted to factors; the rest are numeric. `pnumlbw` and `pnumsga` are 0 for all children, almost all mothers have `parity` = 0 (only 3 do not), and no mother is in the "Other" race group, so these variables carry little or no information.

**Proposed model.** I chose predictors based on a hypothesized structure: factors known before delivery that affect fetal growth. These are gestational age (`gaweeks`), baby's sex (`babysex`), mother's race (`mrace`), smoking (`smoken`), pre-pregnancy BMI (`ppbmi`), and weight gain (`wtgain`). I did not include head circumference or length, since these are measured at birth along with weight. Father’s race is left out because it is highly correlated with mother’s race, and parity is left out because it has almost no variation.

```{r}
my_fit = lm(bwt ~ gaweeks + babysex + mrace + smoken + ppbmi + wtgain, data = bwt_df)

my_fit |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Residuals vs fitted values:

```{r}
resid_plot =
  bwt_df |>
  modelr::add_predictions(my_fit) |>
  modelr::add_residuals(my_fit) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pred, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs fitted values (proposed model)",
    x = "Fitted birthweight (grams)",
    y = "Residual"
  )

resid_plot

ggsave("plots/resid_plot.png", resid_plot, width = 8, height = 5)
```

Residuals are mostly centered around 0 with no clear pattern for fitted values between about 2500 and 3800 grams. At low fitted values (below about 2500 grams) the residuals are more spread out, suggesting the model fits less well for small babies.

Compare with the two other models using cross validation.

```{r}
cv_df =
  crossv_mc(bwt_df, 100) |>
  mutate(
    train = map(train, as_tibble),
    test = map(test, as_tibble)
  )

cv_df =
  cv_df |>
  mutate(
    my_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(bwt ~ gaweeks + babysex + mrace + smoken + ppbmi + wtgain, data = df)),
    main_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(bwt ~ blength + gaweeks, data = df)),
    interaction_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(bwt ~ bhead * blength * babysex, data = df))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    rmse_my = map2_dbl(my_fit, test, rmse),
    rmse_main = map2_dbl(main_fit, test, rmse),
    rmse_interaction = map2_dbl(interaction_fit, test, rmse)
  )
```

```{r}
cv_plot =
  cv_df |>
  select(starts_with("rmse_")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "model",
    names_prefix = "rmse_",
    values_to = "rmse"
  ) |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rmse)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(
    title = "Cross-validated prediction error",
    x = "Model",
    y = "RMSE"
  )

cv_plot

ggsave("plots/cv_plot.png", cv_plot, width = 8, height = 5)
```

The interaction model (head circumference, length, sex and all interactions) has the lowest RMSE (about 290), followed by the main effects model (length and gestational age, about 330). My proposed model has the highest RMSE (about 425) because it does not use body measurements at birth, which are strongly related to birthweight. Therefore, for prediction, the interaction model performs best.
